paragraphs: R' Yaakov bar Avin, or bar Bun — bei R' Bun.
We find that he spoke in the name of R-Sh-B-L in Sheviit, ch. 3, halakhah 5.

And in the name of R-Sh-B-G in Nedarim ch. 3, halakhah 3, Shevuot chapter 3, end of halakhah 8; and in Bereshit Rabbah 4:2 we find R' Pinchas and R' Yaakov bar Avin in the name of R-Sh-B-G. And in Peah ch. 3, halakhah 3, and Eruvin ch. 9, halakhah 3, he spoke in the name of R' Chanina.
And in Yevamot ch. 6, halakhah 7, he spoke in the name of R' Yose bar R' Chanina. And in Vayikra Rabbah ch. 21 he spoke in the name of R' Avin.

Hyman says that in the days of R' Yirmiyah he was already a leader of the generation, as is told in Moed Katan ch. 3, halakhah 1: once they took nazirite vows in Tiberias and needed a large sum of money, and R' Yirmiyah sent to R' Yaakov bar Bun that he should give a silver lamp. He said to him, ‘Yirmiyah has not yet turned back from his evil’ [for he had suffered harm also from the sages], and (R' Yirmiyah) wished to excommunicate him, but R' Chiyya, son of R' Yitzchak Atishya, did not allow him.

And Hyman says R' Zerikin was like a student-colleague of his, as in Eruvin ch. 9, halakhah 3: R' Zerikin said, ‘Many times I walked [or: discussed at length] with R' Yaakov bar Bun and did not hear this matter from him.’

notes.text: The named Moed Katan3:1 paragraph describes distress in Tiberias and a request for a silver lamp; it does not mention nazirite vows or a quantity of spices. Hyman’s supplied נזרו נזירות/סממן therefore remains a substantive source question. “Turned back from his evil” is not recovery from illness. The difficult bracketed gloss is retained as unresolved, not translated as an established event.

The printed notice (volume II, p. 773) reads נזרו נזירות, “they took nazirite vows,” but ממון הרבה, “much money,” beside the supplied סממן. The English follows the printed money reading; the Hebrew source is unchanged. The directly consulted Jerusalem Talmud Moed Katan narrative instead opens with distress upon Tiberias and a request for a silver lamp. It does not independently verify the vows. “Decrees were imposed” was only a proposed reconstruction and is not substituted for the printed vows. The account of an already prominent leader and the description of Zerikin as like a student-colleague remain Hyman’s chronological and relational conclusions. The whole Eruvin 9:3 passage gives the report in Chanina’s name and Zerikan’s statement that many times he explained the matter with Yaakov bar Bun and never heard it from him; the earlier “walked [or: discussed at length]” remains a tentative rendering, not proof of travel. The passage’s subsequent reply is not inserted into Hyman’s excerpt. The house-of form, bar/bei variants and abbreviated titles are retained, and the bracketed explanation concerning the sages remains difficult. Other exact listed witnesses and printings have not been freshly collated; the existing notes remain verbatim beside these new comparisons.
